strengths: The motivation is compelling. Figure 1 provides an explicit example showing why ignoring context or fixing the intervention scope can prevent recovery of the optimal policy.

Combining POMPS selection with contextual GP optimisation is a useful contribution. Averaging historical UCB values offers a sensible mechanism for comparing scopes whose policies improve during learning.

The experiments use 110 random seeds and report uncertainty over 700 interventions. Including settings where the baselines can attain the optimum, alongside noise, backend, and context ablations, strengthens the empirical evidence.
weaknesses: The reduction from general mixed policies to the bandit model is not established. Definition 1 permits an acyclic scope {(X1; ∅), (X2; C)} with X1 → C, where the distribution of C depends on the intervention on X1. Sections 4 and B.1 instead sample contexts from a fixed distribution before selecting the joint action. The paper needs additional restrictions or a sequential treatment to justify its guarantees for the stated causal setting.

The regret proof contains substantive gaps. On page 27, action suboptimality f_i*(c) − f_i(x,c) is bounded by the range of f_i* across contexts. This is false in general: the optimal value can be constant across contexts while an action remains suboptimal. Furthermore, the instance-dependent proof concludes with c(T), defined using worst-arm information gain γ_T, whereas Theorem 1 states a bound using arm-averaged information gain γ̄_T. The stronger stated bound requires justification.

The connection between the analysed algorithm and the implementation is insufficiently demonstrated. The theory assumes independent GP functions, known kernels, compact domains, and independent Gaussian observation noise. HEBO learns transformations, and several experimental SCMs have unbounded Gaussian contexts or confounding-induced non-Gaussian noise. These differences limit the applicability of the guarantees and warrant evaluation of the actual analysed UCB-BO procedure.

The comparisons do not adequately isolate the proposed scope-selection rule. Most evidence comes from a few constructed SCMs, and several comparisons deliberately restrict the baselines so they cannot attain the optimum. The backend and context ablations are useful, but comparisons against alternative selectors using the same POMPS set are missing. Functional causal BO, and other relevant methods on compatible settings, would also strengthen the evaluation.

The scalability claims exceed the evidence. Section 3 explicitly uses exponential brute-force scope enumeration. The large example contains 86 contextual/intervenable variables but only two POMPSs and many redundant variables. It demonstrates useful dimension reduction, while leaving preprocessing cost and scaling with the number of competing scopes untested.

Reproducibility needs substantial improvement. The PDF claims a public implementation but supplies no repository link or numerical experimental settings for β, ρ, and acquisition optimisation. Algorithm 2 lacks an else/continue after initialization, allowing selection over uninitialized arms. Appendix A.1.2 omits Cancer from the PSA equation although the subsequent optimum derivation includes it, and A.3 defines C4 using itself. These inconsistencies prevent unambiguous reconstruction of the algorithm and environments.
